EO 14274 (signed 2025-04-15) revokes EO 12072 and EO 13006, the two orders sec. 6(c) reinstated; it does not name EO 14091, takes effect after the first end and ends no EO 14091 clause, and the dossier holds no evidence id for it, so it is recorded in the clause reason of sec. 6(c) and in savings_residuals rather than attached. The OFR notes on EO 14091 itself name only EO 14148 as acting on it. The conflict NO_ORDER_CITED_IN_CURRENT_LAW (2 CFR 200.318 citation) was read and resolved. savings_residuals.reason: Reading record LSP-EO_14148 (reused from Lambertini II after re-verifying text_sha256 65bf2d86...): sec. 2 revokes 78 listed actions with no effective-date wording, so each revocation took effect on signing 2025-01-20; sec. 3 directs agencies to end implementation, tells the DPC and NEC Directors to review and rescind actions taken under the listed orders, and the NSA to review NSMs; sec. 4(a) is a no-impair clause for statutory authority and OMB functions only; there is no successor delegation, transfer of functions, funds or property, pending-matter clause or exception for any listed order, and no revival wording. Own-residual check, reading EO 14091 in full (secs. 1-11): it created Agency Equity Teams and the White House Steering Committee on Equity (sec. 2), required annual Equity Action Plans (sec. 3), directed agency and OMB actions (secs. 4-5, 8), set the FY2025 15 percent SDB procurement goal (sec. 7), assigned the OSTP subcommittee reports (sec. 9) and, in sec. 6(c), revoked EO 13946 and EO 13853 and reinstated EO 12072 and EO 13006 'as they were prior to issuance of Executive Order 13946'. Residuals: the revocations of EO 13946 and EO 13853 are completed acts that EO 14148 does not undo (no revival wording), so they accrued and remain; the reinstatement of EO 12072 and EO 13006 was an executed act whose products were separate orders that EO 14148 did not touch and that stayed in force after 2025-01-20 until EO 14274 (2025-04-15; held text read) revoked both in its sec. 2(a)-(b); EO 14274 does not name EO 14091 and does not revive EO 13946, so at the 2026-10-14 cutoff only the completed revocations remain as the residual. The Teams and the Committee are offices that depend on the order, so they ended with it. No function, fund or property was transferred. Prefill 'review' (S4 conflict): the conflict was read and resolved (see conflict_resolutions) and the prefill overruled to transferred_or_accrued. Executive Order 14148 of January 20, 2025 
Initial Rescissions of Harmful Executive Orders and Actions 
By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the 
laws of the United States of America, it is hereby ordered as follows: 
Section 1. Purpose and Policy. The previous administration has embedded 
deeply unpopular, inflationary, illegal, and radical practices within every 
agency and office of the Federal Government. The injection of ‘‘diversity, 
equity, and inclusion’’ (DEI) into our institutions has corrupted them by 
replacing hard work, merit, and equality with a divisive and dangerous 
preferential hierarchy. Orders to open the borders have endangered the 
American people and dissolved Federal, State, and local resources that should 
be used to benefit the American people. Climate extremism has exploded 
inflation and overburdened businesses with regulation. 
To commence the policies that will make our Nation united, fair, safe, 
and prosperous again, it is the policy of the United States to restore common 
sense to the Federal Government and unleash the potential of the American 
citizen. The revocations within this order will be the first of many steps 
the United States Federal Government will take to repair our institutions 
and our economy. 
Sec. 2. Revocation of Orders and Actions. The following executive actions 
are hereby revoked: 
(a) Executive Order 13985 of January 20, 2021 (Advancing Racial Equity 
and Support for Underserved Communities Through the Federal Govern-
ment). 
(b) Executive Order 13986 of January 20, 2021 (Ensuring a Lawful and 
Accurate Enumeration and Apportionment Pursuant to the Decennial Cen-
sus).

the United States Government To Provide a Unified and Effective Response 
To Combat COVID–19 and To Provide United States Leadership on Global 
Health and Security).

Discrimination on the Basis of Gender Identity or Sexual Orientation).

Executive Branch Personnel).

and the Environment and Restoring Science To Tackle the Climate Crisis).

force for COVID–19 and Other Biological Threats).

Access to Care and Treatments for COVID–19).

Sec. 1(b) rewrote sec. 3(f) of EO 12866 (the definition of 'significant regulatory action'). EO 12866 is not revoked and EO 14148 has no wording restoring the former text of sec. 3(f), so the rewritten text is a residual in a living order, recorded under savings_residuals as continuing_independent; the clause is treated as ended as an instrument of EO 14094.

later_events.mechanism: EO 14215 sec. 3(a) amends sec. 3(b) of EO 12866 'as amended' (the definition of 'Agency'), a different paragraph from the sec. 3(f) that EO 14094 sec. 1(b) rewrote; it does not name EO 14094, has no effective-date wording so takes effect on signing 2025-02-18, which is after EO 14148 sec. 2(ddd) had revoked EO 14094 on 2025-01-20, so it ends nothing here and does not move the first end

operative_clauses.original_operative_text:
Sec. 2. Affirmative Promotion of Inclusive Regulatory Policy and Public 
Participation. (a) To the extent practicable and consistent with applicable 
law, regulatory actions should be informed by input from interested or 
affected communities; State, local, territorial, and Tribal officials and agen-
cies; interested or affected parties in the private sector and other regulated 
entities; those with expertise in relevant disciplines; and the public as 
a whole. Opportunities for public participation shall be designed to promote 
equitable and meaningful participation by a range of interested or affected 
parties, including underserved communities.

operative_clauses.original_operative_text:
(c) To inform the development of regulatory agendas and plans, agencies 
shall endeavor, as practicable and appropriate, to proactively engage inter-
ested or affected parties, including members of underserved communities; 
consumers; workers and labor organizations; program beneficiaries; busi-
nesses and regulated entities; those with expertise in relevant disciplines; 
and other parties that may be interested or affected. These efforts shall 
incorporate, to the extent consistent with applicable law, best practices 
for information accessibility and engagement with interested or affected 
parties, including, as practicable and appropriate, community-based outreach; 
outreach to organizations that work with interested or affected parties; use 
of agency field offices; use of alternative platforms and media for engaging 
the public; and expansion of public capacity for engaging in the rulemaking 
process.

operative_clauses.original_operative_text:
(ii) Implement reforms to improve procedures and policies with respect 
to OIRA’s consideration of meeting requests initiated by persons not em-
ployed by the executive branch of the Federal Government regarding the 
substance of regulatory actions under OIRA review to further the efficiency 
and effectiveness of such meetings. These reforms may include: 
(A) efforts to ensure access for meeting requesters who have not histori-
cally requested such meetings; 
(B) discouraging meeting requests that are duplicative of earlier meetings 
with OIRA regarding the same regulatory action by the same meeting 
requesters; 
(C) consolidation of meetings by requester, subject matter, or any other 
consistently applied factors deemed appropriate to improve efficiency and 
effectiveness; and 
(D) disclosure of data in an open, machine-readable, and accessible 
format that includes the dates and names of individuals involved in all 
substantive meetings and the subject matter discussed during such meet-
ings, as required by section 6(b)(4)(C)(iii) of Executive Order 12866, so 
as to better facilitate transparency and analysis.

Sec. 3. Improving Regulatory Analysis. (a) Regulatory analysis should facili-
tate agency efforts to develop regulations that serve the public interest, 
advance statutory objectives, and are consistent with Executive Order 12866, 
Executive Order 13563, and the Presidential Memorandum of January 20, 
2021 (Modernizing Regulatory Review). Regulatory analysis, as practicable 
and appropriate, shall recognize distributive impacts and equity, to the 
extent permitted by law.

Title 3— 
The President 
Executive Order 14094 of April 6, 2023 
Modernizing Regulatory Review 
By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the 
laws of the United States of America, and in order to modernize the regulatory 
process to advance policies that promote the public interest and address 
national priorities, it is hereby ordered as follows: 
Section 1. Improving the Effectiveness of the Regulatory Review Process. 
(a) This order supplements and reaffirms the principles, structures, and 
definitions governing contemporary regulatory review established in Execu-
tive Order 12866 of September 30, 1993 (Regulatory Planning and Review), 
and Executive Order 13563 of January 18, 2011 (Improving Regulation and 
Regulatory Review). Any provisions of those orders not amended in this 
order shall remain in effect. This order also further implements the Presi-
dential Memorandum of January 20, 2021 (Modernizing Regulatory Review). 
(b) Section 3(f) of Executive Order 12866 is hereby amended to read 
as follows: 
‘‘(f) ‘‘Significant regulatory action’’ means any regulatory action that is 
likely to result in a rule that may: 
(1) have an annual effect on the economy of $200 million or more 
(adjusted every 3 years by the Administrator of OIRA for changes in 
gross domestic product); or adversely affect in a material way the 
economy, a sector of the economy, productivity, competition, jobs, the 
environment, public health or safety, or State, local, territorial, or trib-
al governments or communities; 
(2) create a serious inconsistency or otherwise interfere with an action 
taken or planned by another agency; 
(3) materially alter the budgetary impact of entitlements, grants, user 
fees, or loan programs or the rights and obligations of recipients there-
of; or 
(4) raise legal or policy issues for which centralized review would 
meaningfully further the President’s priorities or the principles set 
forth in this Executive order, as specifically authorized in a timely 
manner by the Administrator of OIRA in each case.’’ 
Sec. 2. Affirmative Promotion of Inclusive Regulatory Policy and Public 
Participation. (a) To the extent practicable and consistent with applicable 
law, regulatory actions should be informed by input from interested or 
affected communities; State, local, territorial, and Tribal officials and agen-
cies; interested or affected parties in the private sector and other regulated 
entities; those with expertise in relevant disciplines; and the public as 
a whole. Opportunities for public participation shall be designed to promote 
equitable and meaningful participation by a range of interested or affected 
parties, including underserved communities. 
(b) To inform the regulatory planning process, executive departments and 
agencies (agencies) shall, to the extent practicable and consistent with appli-
cable law: 
(i) clarify opportunities for interested persons to petition for the issuance, 
amendment, or repeal of a rule under 5 U.S.C. 553(e); 
(ii) endeavor to respond to such petitions efficiently, in light of agency 
judgments of available resources and priorities; and 
(iii) maintain, subject to available resources, a log of such petitions re-
ceived, and share with the Administrator of the Office of Information

and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), upon request, information on the status

(c) To inform the development of regulatory agendas and plans, agencies 
shall endeavor, as practicable and appropriate, to proactively engage inter-
ested or affected parties, including members of underserved communities; 
consumers; workers and labor organizations; program beneficiaries; busi-
nesses and regulated entities; those with expertise in relevant disciplines; 
and other parties that may be interested or affected. These efforts shall 
incorporate, to the extent consistent with applicable law, best practices 
for information accessibility and engagement with interested or affected 
parties, including, as practicable and appropriate, community-based outreach; 
outreach to organizations that work with interested or affected parties; use 
of agency field offices; use of alternative platforms and media for engaging 
the public; and expansion of public capacity for engaging in the rulemaking 
process. 
(d) The Administrator of OIRA, in consultation with relevant agencies, 
as appropriate, shall consider guidance or tools to modernize the notice- 
and-comment process, including through technological changes. These re-
forms may include guidance or tools to address mass comments, computer- 
generated comments (such as those generated through artificial intelligence), 
and falsely attributed comments. 
(e) Section 6(b)(4) of Executive Order 12866 establishes a process for 
persons not employed by the executive branch of the Federal Government 
to request meetings with OIRA officials regarding the substance of regulatory 
actions under OIRA review. Public trust in the regulatory process depends 
on protecting regulatory development from the risk or appearance of disparate 
and undue influence, including in the OIRA review process. In order to 
reduce this risk or appearance, the Administrator of OIRA shall, to the 
extent practicable and consistent with applicable law: 
(i) Provide information to facilitate the initiation of meeting requests regard-
ing regulatory actions under OIRA review from potential participants not 
employed by the executive branch of the Federal Government who have 
not historically requested such meetings, including those from underserved 
communities; and 
(ii) Implement reforms to improve procedures and policies with respect 
to OIRA’s consideration of meeting requests initiated by persons not em-
ployed by the executive branch of the Federal Government regarding the 
substance of regulatory actions under OIRA review to further the efficiency 
and effectiveness of such meetings. These reforms may include: 
(A) efforts to ensure access for meeting requesters who have not histori-
cally requested such meetings; 
(B) discouraging meeting requests that are duplicative of earlier meetings 
with OIRA regarding the same regulatory action by the same meeting 
requesters; 
(C) consolidation of meetings by requester, subject matter, or any other 
consistently applied factors deemed appropriate to improve efficiency and 
effectiveness; and 
(D) disclosure of data in an open, machine-readable, and accessible 
format that includes the dates and names of individuals involved in all 
substantive meetings and the subject matter discussed during such meet-
ings, as required by section 6(b)(4)(C)(iii) of Executive Order 12866, so 
as to better facilitate transparency and analysis. 
Sec. 3. Improving Regulatory Analysis. (a) Regulatory analysis should facili-
tate agency efforts to develop regulations that serve the public interest, 
advance statutory objectives, and are consistent with Executive Order 12866, 
Executive Order 13563, and the Presidential Memorandum of January 20, 
2021 (Modernizing Regulatory Review). Regulatory analysis, as practicable 
and appropriate, shall recognize distributive impacts and equity, to the 
extent permitted by law.

research_rationale: EO 14094 (signed 2023-04-06, 88 FR 21879-21881), read in full from the held official FR text: sec. 1(a) reaffirms EO 12866 and EO 13563; sec. 1(b) rewrites sec. 3(f) of EO 12866; sec. 2 inclusive regulatory policy and public participation; sec. 3 regulatory analysis and the Circular A-4 revision; sec. 4 general provisions. No term or sunset. EO 14148 sec. 2(ddd) (reading record LSP-EO_14148) revokes it in full effective on signing 2025-01-20, no effective-date wording, no exception. The dossier's 24 clauses cover secs. 1-4(c) to the signature line with no gap. Leads read: the dossier's other-actor provision ACT:EO:14094>EO:14215 is EO 14215 sec. 3(a) amending sec. 3(b) of EO 12866 'as amended'; read in the held text, it names neither EO 14094 nor sec. 3(f), so it is attached to the sec. 1 clauses as a later event that ends nothing here (signed 2025-02-18, after the first end). The dossier 'target provision not located' lines for EO 12866 and EO 13563 are OFR 'See' cross-references. The conflict NO_ORDER_CITED_IN_CURRENT_LAW was read and resolved as the sec. 1(b) text embedded in EO 12866. Savings: continuing_independent (the rewritten sec. 3(f) of EO 12866).

savings_residuals.reason: Reading record LSP-EO_14148 (reused from Lambertini II after re-verifying text_sha256 65bf2d86...): sec. 2 revokes 78 listed actions with no effective-date wording, so each revocation took effect on signing 2025-01-20; sec. 3 directs agencies to end implementation, tells the DPC and NEC Directors to review and rescind actions taken under the listed orders, and the NSA to review NSMs; sec. 4(a) is a no-impair clause for statutory authority and OMB functions only; there is no successor delegation, transfer of functions, funds or property, pending-matter clause or exception for any listed order, and no revival wording. Own-residual check, reading EO 14094 in full (secs. 1-4): sec. 1(a) reaffirms EO 12866 and EO 13563; sec. 1(b) rewrites sec. 3(f) of EO 12866 (annual-effect threshold of $200 million, adjusted every 3 years, and the other limbs of 'significant regulatory action'); secs. 2-3 direct agencies and OIRA on public participation and regulatory analysis, including revising OMB Circular A-4 within one year; sec. 4 is general provisions. The sec. 1(b) text now sits inside EO 12866, which EO 14148 does not revoke, and EO 14148 contains no wording restoring the former sec. 3(f), so the rewritten paragraph is a residual that the revocation of EO 14094 does not cancel on its face. The OLRC note at 5 U.S.C. 601 note, which prints EO 12866 'as amended', still lists 'Ex. Ord. No. 14094, sec. 1(b)' among its amendments next to EO 14215 sec. 3(a) (current-law lead, snippet only, no held legal-text slice), and later orders (EO 14192, 14219, 14267) cite EO 12866 'as amended' without restoring sec. 3(f). Whether OIRA applies the $200 million threshold or the earlier one is a question this claim does not decide. The remaining secs. 2-3 directions and the Circular A-4 revision (an OMB document the order told OMB to issue) are agency actions outside the order. No transfer of functions, funds or property. Prefill 'review' (S4 conflict, own_savings_lead true): overruled to continuing_independent on the embedded amendment. Bounded search: every held official FR text was grepped for 14094 (only EO 14148 names it) and every held order of 2025 or later was grepped for 12866 (EO 14192, 14215, 14219, 14267, 14294) for any rewrite of sec. 3(f) (none), OFR catalog edges and the OLRC notes at 5 U.S.C. 601 note were read.

Executive Order 14148 of January 20, 2025 
Initial Rescissions of Harmful Executive Orders and Actions 
By the authority vested in me as President by the Constitution and the 
laws of the United States of America, it is hereby ordered as follows: 
Section 1. Purpose and Policy. The previous administration has embedded 
deeply unpopular, inflationary, illegal, and radical practices within every 
agency and office of the Federal Government. The injection of ‘‘diversity, 
equity, and inclusion’’ (DEI) into our institutions has corrupted them by 
replacing hard work, merit, and equality with a divisive and dangerous 
preferential hierarchy. Orders to open the borders have endangered the 
American people and dissolved Federal, State, and local resources that should 
be used to benefit the American people. Climate extremism has exploded 
inflation and overburdened businesses with regulation. 
To commence the policies that will make our Nation united, fair, safe, 
and prosperous again, it is the policy of the United States to restore common 
sense to the Federal Government and unleash the potential of the American 
citizen. The revocations within this order will be the first of many steps 
the United States Federal Government will take to repair our institutions 
and our economy. 
Sec. 2. Revocation of Orders and Actions. The following executive actions 
are hereby revoked: 
(a) Executive Order 13985 of January 20, 2021 (Advancing Racial Equity 
and Support for Underserved Communities Through the Federal Govern-

(b) The Director of the Domestic Policy Council (DPC) and the Director

actions taken pursuant to the orders, memoranda, and proclamations listed 
in section 2 of this order and take necessary steps to rescind, replace,

order, the Director of the DPC and the Director of the NEC shall submit 
to the President an additional list of orders, memoranda, and proclamations 
issued by the prior administration that should be rescinded, as well as 
a list of replacement orders, memoranda, or proclamations, to increase Amer-
ican prosperity. 
(c) The National Security Advisor (NSA) shall immediately begin a com-
plete and thorough review of all National Security Memoranda (NSMs) issued 
from January 20, 2021, through January 20, 2025, for harm to national 
security, domestic resilience, and American values. No later than 45 days 
from the date of this order, the NSA shall recommend to the President 
NSMs for rescission. 
Sec. 4. General Provisions. (a) Nothing in this order shall be construed 
to impair or otherwise affect: 
(i) the authority granted by law to an executive department or agency, 
or the head thereof; or 
(ii) the functions of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget 
relating to budgetary, administrative, or legislative proposals. 
(b) This order shall be implemented consistent with applicable law and 
subject to the availability of appropriations. 
(c) This order is not intended to, and does not, create any right or benefit, 
substantive or procedural, enforceable at law or in equity by any party 
against the United States, its departments, agencies, or entities, its officers, 
employees, or agents, or any other person.
